Information received since the FOMC met in November indicates continued labor-market strength and solid economic activity, while inflation remains below 2 percent. In the literature, a Phillips-curve framework with forward-looking expectations (e.g., Woodford; Svensson’s inflation-forecast targeting) implies that with tight labor markets and anchored expectations, inflation should gradually move toward target, supporting the Committee’s gradualism. Simple policy rules in the Taylor (1983/1993) tradition would also justify measured rate increases when the output gap is positive and inflation is near—but below—target. However, Orphanides’ real-time mismeasurement critique warns that misjudging slack can lead to overtightening when inflation is subdued. Empirically, monetary tightening is associated with weaker future consumption growth (Canzoneri, Cumby, and Diba, 2007), which tempers the otherwise positive tone. The emphasis on a symmetric 2 percent objective and careful monitoring of inflation is consistent with the time-inconsistency literature and Rogoff’s “conservative central banker” rationale for price-stability credibility. Net assessment: moderately positive but cautious.
